## Where we are going

- Apply analogous, parametric, and bottom-up estimating and state each one's error profile.
- Build a cost baseline including contingency and management reserve, and place each correctly.
- Explain estimate ranges as a function of project phase.

---

## The frame

| Method | Basis | Typical accuracy | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| Analogous (top-down) | Similar past project, scaled | −25% to +75% | Concept phase, minutes of effort |
| Parametric | Statistical model on a driver (cost/m², cost/function point) | −15% to +30% | When you have a calibrated model |
| Bottom-up (definitive) | Sum of work packages | −5% to +10% | After a validated WBS; expensive |
| Three-point | (o + 4m + p)/6 per element | Depends | Layers on any of the above |

---

## The argument

- Estimating methods
- Cost baseline structure — get this ordering right, students always garble it:
- Funding limit reconciliation

---

## Check yourself

1. Your bottom-up estimate is 12% below your parametric estimate. Which do you trust and what do you do?
2. A risk you identified materializes. Which reserve pays for it, and who approves?
3. Why can't you produce a ±5% estimate at project initiation, no matter how skilled you are?
4. What happens to EV metrics if management reserve is accidentally included in the baseline?

---

## Somewhere else entirely

**Insurance underwriting.** An underwriter doesn't estimate whether *your* house will burn; they price a portfolio using base rates and hold reserves against the distribution. Contingency reserve is the loss-cost provision; management reserve is capital held against tail events. Ask why project sponsors resist the framing that actuaries take for granted.
